title: Risk Assessments: Apply ISO and NIST in 90 Days for Security Teams
summary: Turn ISO 31000 and NIST guidance into a 90 day risk assessment roadmap. Set scope, score exposure, document findings, and keep security teams aligned.
body_markdown:
A risk assessment is the process of identifying, analyzing, and evaluating risks against criteria set before the work begins, and the first thing we recommend doing is setting that scope and those criteria so the assessment produces a prioritized risk register rather than a list of guesses. This approach draws on[ISO 31000](https://erm.ncsu.edu/resource-center/isos-risk-management-framework/) and[NIST SP 800-30](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/30/r1/final) , both of which treat assessment as a structured, repeatable discipline rather than a one-time exercise.


---


> **TL;DR:**
>
>
> - Define scope, appetite, and concrete likelihood and impact anchors before scoring; otherwise, scores vary by workshop and cannot support defensible decisions.
> - Use a risk matrix to triage the full inventory, then reserve Monte Carlo modeling for high ranked financial or schedule risks with adequate historical data.
> - Record inherent and residual scores, test controls, and assign each risk an owner, treatment deadline, review date, and trigger for amber or red indicators.
> - Organizations should review the full register annually, refresh highest risk areas quarterly, and reassess after any material business or technology change.

## Why risk assessments matter in the risk management lifecycle


Under ISO 31000:2018, risk assessment is the analytical core of the broader risk management process. It consists of three mandatory steps: identification (what could happen), analysis (how likely and how severe), and evaluation (whether the risk is acceptable against defined criteria). Everything else, including monitoring and communication, wraps around this core.


The output matters as much as the process. A well-run assessment gives leadership a ranked view of exposure, which feeds directly into decisions about risk appetite, where to invest in controls, and which risks to transfer, reduce, or simply accept. Without that ranked view, boards are asked to approve budgets and sign-offs based on anecdote rather than evidence.


Organizations that run assessments consistently tend to see three practical benefits: sharper justification for control spending, board reporting that holds up under scrutiny, and faster, calmer response when an incident actually happens because the scenario was already mapped. None of that requires elaborate tooling at the start. It requires defined scope, defined criteria, and a habit of writing things down the same way every time.


## Which standards should guide your assessment: ISO 31000, ISO/IEC 31010, and NIST


Two reference families cover most of what practitioners need. ISO 31000 describes the risk management process at the enterprise level: establish context, identify, analyze, evaluate, treat, monitor. Its companion standard, ISO/IEC 31010:2019, catalogues more than 40 distinct assessment techniques, from basic brainstorming to Monte Carlo simulation, so teams can match the technique to the risk type and the data they actually have.


For information systems, the NIST Risk Management Framework offers a seven-stage lifecycle: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor. It pushes toward near real-time risk management and continuous monitoring rather than point-in-time snapshots, which matters for systems that change weekly.


In practice, the two sit well together. Enterprise and operational risk teams tend to use ISO 31000 for context and governance, while security and IT teams layer NIST RMF on top for system-level assessment and ongoing monitoring. Our guide on[choosing an IT risk management framework](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/information-technology-risk-management-framework) walks through how to blend the two without duplicating effort.


## Choosing a methodology: qualitative, quantitative, and everything between


The right methodology depends on the data you have and who will read the output. Qualitative methods use descriptive scales (low, medium, high) and expert judgment, which makes them fast but more subjective. Quantitative methods assign numeric values, dollar exposure, or probability distributions, which takes more data and analytical skill but produces results that hold up in financial or board-level discussions. Semi-quantitative approaches sit in between, scoring likelihood and impact on numbered scales without pretending to full statistical rigor.


Several named techniques cover most practical needs:


- A **risk matrix** plots likelihood against impact for fast, visual triage across a large risk population.
- **Bow-tie analysis** maps causes on one side and consequences on the other, which is useful when you need to see every control sitting between a threat and its impact.
- **Monte Carlo simulation** models a range of outcomes for financial or schedule risk when you have enough historical data to build a distribution.
- **Scenario analysis** stress-tests strategic assumptions against plausible future events rather than scoring a single static risk.


Most teams mix methods rather than picking one. A common pattern is to run a quick matrix across the full risk population, then apply quantitative modeling only to the handful of risks that rank highest, since that is where the extra effort pays off. Our[overview of risk management methods](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/methods-for-risk-management) covers treatment options once the scoring is done.


## How to run a risk assessment step by step


A repeatable playbook turns assessment from a one-off workshop into something you can defend to an auditor or a board. The steps below follow the same logic as ISO 31000 and SP 800-30, adapted into a sequence a working team can actually execute.


1. **Set scope and context.** Define what is in and out of scope, confirm the organization's risk appetite, and get sign-off from stakeholders before anyone identifies a single risk.
2. **Agree on criteria and scales.** Fix your likelihood and impact scales and write down what each point means in concrete terms, not adjectives alone.
3. **Identify risks.** Run structured workshops, use checklists and asset inventories, review incident history, and consider a pre-mortem exercise where the team imagines a failure and works backward to its causes.
4. **Analyze each risk.** Score likelihood and impact, test whether existing controls actually work as designed, and record both inherent risk (before controls) and residual risk (after controls).
5. **Evaluate against criteria.** Compare each scored risk to your appetite statement and decide: accept, reduce, transfer, or avoid. Assign an owner and a deadline to every decision.
6. **Build treatment plans.** Turn each decision into a SMART action: specific, measurable, assigned, realistic, time-bound, with a named owner and a trigger that tells you when the treatment is working or failing.
7. **Document and review.** Populate the risk register, generate a heat map, write a board brief, and set a review date before you close the exercise out.


**Pro Tip:** *Write your likelihood and impact scale definitions down once, in plain language, and reuse the exact same wording in every workshop. That single habit does more for consistency than any new software ever will.*


The deliverables that matter at the end are a populated risk register with named owners, a heat map that visualizes concentration of exposure, a board-ready brief, and an action-tracking plan with dates attached.[NIST IR 8286A](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2025/NIST.IR.8286Ar1.pdf) recommends documenting cybersecurity risk scenarios directly in the enterprise risk register so technical findings reach the same decision-makers who see operational and financial risk, rather than living in a separate security-only document.


## Matching tools and techniques to your team's data and skill


Technique choice is partly a data question and partly a resourcing question. Simple matrices work for triage across a large risk inventory because they need the least data and the least specialized skill. Bow-tie diagrams are worth the extra setup time when a risk has a genuinely complex cause-and-effect path, such as a supply chain disruption with multiple failure points. Monte Carlo simulation earns its cost only when you are modeling financial or schedule tail risk and have enough historical data to build a credible distribution.


Whatever tool you land on, a few features matter regardless of methodology: version control so you can see how a risk score changed over time, an audit trail that shows who changed what and when, dashboards for key risk indicators, role-based access so sensitive risk data stays with the right people, and exportable evidence that an authorizing official can actually use in a sign-off package. A spreadsheet can satisfy all of these at small scale. Larger, recurring assessment programs tend to outgrow spreadsheets once the audit trail and access control requirements get serious, and that is a resourcing decision worth making deliberately rather than by accident.


## Scoring likelihood, impact, and the gap between inherent and residual risk


Subjectivity creeps in wherever scales are vague. Build scales for both likelihood and impact, and write an explicit anchor for every point: what does a given likelihood level actually look like, in a sentence, not just a label.


Score every risk twice. Inherent risk is what the exposure looks like with no controls in place. Residual risk is what remains after your existing controls are applied, and testing whether those controls genuinely work (not just whether they exist on paper) is what makes the residual score honest.


Key risk indicators turn a static score into something you monitor continuously. Pick a small number of indicators tied directly to your highest-ranked risks, set green, amber, and red thresholds for each, and link every amber or red reading to a specific treatment trigger, not just a notification.


## What to document: risk register fields, heat maps, and board evidence


A risk register earns its keep only if it has the right fields and someone keeps it current. At minimum, include:


- **Risk ID and description** , with a clear cause, event, and consequence written as a single sentence.
- **Likelihood and impact scores** , both inherent and residual, using your defined scale.
- **Existing controls** and an honest note on whether they are tested or assumed.
- **Owner and treatment actions** , each with a deadline and a status.
- **Review date** , so nobody has to guess when the risk was last looked at.


For boards, compress the register into an executive summary: the highest-ranked risks by residual score, what changed since the last review, and what decision you need from them. That page, paired with the heat map, is usually the evidence an authorizing official needs to sign off on a control investment or accept a residual exposure. Reporting cadence should match audience: operational teams may want a monthly register refresh, while boards typically need a quarterly or semiannual summary unless a material event forces an earlier conversation.


## How often to reassess, and how maturity models keep the program honest


Cadence should follow risk, not the calendar alone. An annual baseline review covers the full register, a quarterly refresh makes sense for your highest-risk areas, and any material change in business or technology should trigger an out-of-cycle reassessment regardless of where you are in the schedule. Cybersecurity and compliance guidance in several jurisdictions, including[New York's DFS cybersecurity regulation](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/industry_letters/il20260910-cyber-risk-assessment) , requires at least annual review plus reassessment after material change, which is a reasonable floor even outside regulated sectors.


[Internal audit guidance](https://iia-p.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/IPPF-PG-Assessing-the-Risk-Management-Process.pdf) recommends benchmarking your process against a maturity model and recording risks in a matrix with impact and likelihood columns, which helps internal audit tailor its own engagements and translate technical findings into strategic terms senior leadership can act on. Tie every assessment cycle back to your appetite statement explicitly, and escalate anything that breaches it rather than letting it sit quietly in the register.


## A plan to stand up your first risk register and KRI dashboard


Days 1 to 30: confirm governance, scope, and risk criteria, select a pilot area, and finalize your likelihood and impact scales. Days 31 to 60: run identification workshops, analyze the top risks, and draft treatment plans with named owners. Days 61 to 90: launch a KRI dashboard, deliver a board-ready brief, and plan the rollout beyond the pilot. Success looks like a complete register, every risk with a named owner, baseline KRI thresholds set, and a working first dashboard. Our piece on[optimizing the risk assessment workflow](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/optimize-risk-assessment-workflow-security) expands on each phase.


## The one habit that separates defensible assessments from guesswork


The mistake we see most often is skipping the upfront definition of risk criteria and appetite and jumping straight to scoring. Without that foundation, every score is relative to whoever is in the room that day, and the assessment falls apart the moment someone challenges it.


The fix is simple to state and easy to neglect: write your scoring anchors down once, keep a single authoritative risk register with version history, and name an owner for every risk, not just every action.


> *— Gaspard*

## FAQ


### What are the 4 types of risk assessment?


Common approaches include qualitative, quantitative, semi-quantitative, and generic or scenario-based assessment. Qualitative uses descriptive scales and expert judgment, quantitative assigns numeric or monetary values, semi-quantitative scores risks on numbered scales without full statistical modeling, and scenario-based assessment stress-tests specific situations such as a system failure or supply disruption.


### What is the risk management assessment?


A risk management assessment is the process of identifying, analyzing, and evaluating risks against pre-defined criteria so an organization can decide how to treat each one. Under ISO 31000, this analytical step sits at the core of the broader risk management process, feeding directly into treatment decisions and board reporting.


### What are the 5 things a risk assessment should include?


A thorough risk assessment should include risk identification, likelihood and impact analysis, evaluation against defined criteria, a treatment plan with named owners, and documentation such as a risk register and review date. Internal audit guidance also recommends recording each risk in a matrix with impact and likelihood columns to determine significance.


### What are the 4 C's of risk assessments?


Definitions of the "4 C's" vary by industry and source, so there is no single standardized version. A common framing used in some workplace safety contexts covers Competence, Cooperation, Communication, and Control, referring to who is involved, how they work together, how findings are shared, and what controls are put in place to manage the risk.


### How often should a risk assessment be reviewed?


Most organizations run a full annual baseline review, with a quarterly refresh for their highest-risk areas. Material changes in business or technology should trigger an immediate reassessment regardless of schedule, a requirement echoed in New York's DFS cybersecurity guidance.
